The volunteers who helped establish Stellaland now present their promises of land to the officials at Vryburg. On paper the grants look simple. On the ground, boundaries cross grazing routes, water sources and claims already held by Tswana communities. Surveyors and interpreters could put the competing accounts before one commission, at a cost the young treasury can scarcely welcome. Confirming the volunteers' grants immediately would reward the men on whom the republic depends, but a title bearing our seal cannot by itself settle the question of who may use the land. The raad must choose whose claims it will hear before the survey pegs become another cause of conflict.
Survey the claims together before issuing titles.
Honour the grants promised to our volunteers.

At Rooigrond, the authority of Goshen reaches into a frontier already shaped by rival Barolong claims and alliances. Farmers want secure grazing, traders want a road they can use, and the commandants want their services recognised by the new government. Negotiation would require us to treat neighbouring authorities as partners whose consent matters, rather than as obstacles to a line drawn on a map. An armed posture may impress the burghers who founded the republic, but it also makes every disputed herd and waterhole a test of sovereignty. Our small administration cannot afford to mistake a show of strength for a lasting settlement.
Secure grazing and passage by agreement.

The union of Stellaland and Goshen has brought two small republics beneath one political roof, without making their accounts agree. Officials still collect revenue for their own districts, while each raad expects the other to contribute to common expenses. A federal budget would show what the union can actually afford and give its officers a single set of instructions. It would also require local leaders to surrender part of the control they exercised before union. Keeping separate accounts is easier for those leaders, but leaves the federal government bargaining for money whenever a shared obligation falls due.
One union requires a common budget.

The move from Ohrigstad to Lydenburg has given the eastern settlers a new centre, but a town is more than a name on the raad's papers. Illness, difficult routes and the distance between farms have exposed the limits of a government carried from one settlement to another. Roads, records and basic public services would help Lydenburg hold its scattered district together. Such work must also contend with existing African settlements and claims, which do not vanish when a Boer farm is registered. The treasury can support a more durable town administration, or leave its growth to the means and initiative of individual households.
Give the new town roads and public services.
Let the farms support their own development.
A small raad on the Buffalo frontier

Utrecht's small raad governs beside a much stronger Zulu kingdom, and its security depends on more than the number of burghers it can muster. Agreements about land and cattle must be understood on both sides of the frontier. A missing interpreter or two different accounts of a boundary can turn an ordinary grazing dispute into an accusation of trespass. Maintaining written records and officials able to negotiate would make the republic's position less dependent on personal understandings. The commandants consider that an unnecessary expense, confident that local knowledge and an armed following will serve better than another office.
Keep interpreters and an agreed boundary record.

The Klein Vrystaat's claim to self-government rests on a concession from the Swazi monarchy, yet the meaning of that concession remains disputed. Settlers speak of ownership where the court may understand a grant with continuing obligations. The republic is too small to disregard either that disagreement or Pretoria's growing influence. Renewed negotiations would cost money and require us to hear the court's account of the arrangement. Seeking Transvaal patronage offers political support instead, but risks convincing our neighbours that a local concession has become an instrument of outside expansion.
Seek a renewed understanding with the Swazi court.
A meeting place beyond the Orange

Beyond the Orange River, the trek parties have found a meeting place at Winburg, but agreement among their leaders is harder to secure than a campsite. Disputes over farms, grazing and service in the commandos arrive before men whose authority rests as much on personal loyalty as on written rules. A permanent volksraad would keep records, hear competing claims and make the commandants answer to a common assembly. Its clerks and meetings would cost money, and the burghers would expect a greater voice in public affairs. Leaving authority with the commandants would preserve a quicker military response, but also the divided administration of a society still organised around its trek leaders.
Let a permanent raad speak for Winburg.

Along the Mooi River, wagons and cattle already bring people together more reliably than official proclamations. A regular market would give farmers a place to sell produce and obtain supplies, while a land register would let the administration resolve claims with something firmer than memory. Traders argue that the settlement can become a centre for the surrounding farms if the raad will pay for this modest institutional foundation. Many burghers remain wary of public expense and the officials who follow it. Potchefstroom can invest in a town economy, or keep its administration small and leave commerce to private arrangements.
Give the market and land register public support.
Keep government small and leave trade to the burghers.

Below the northern mountains, the settlement's fortunes depend on routes that run through country governed by African rulers and communities. Ivory, cattle and imported goods cannot travel safely on the strength of a proclamation from our raad alone. Interpreters and negotiated access would help merchants maintain their connections and give disputes somewhere to be heard before they become reprisals. Some burghers instead demand exclusive authority over the district, treating recognition of neighbouring claims as a surrender of their own. Such a declaration may strengthen their confidence in the government, while deepening the resentment of those expected to submit to it.
Employ interpreters and keep the trading routes open.
Assert the exclusive authority of the burghers.

The Klip River settlers have proclaimed a government of their own, but the British authorities regard Natal as territory already under their jurisdiction. A small raad cannot make that disagreement disappear by writing another constitution. Accommodation might preserve local influence over farms and district affairs, at the expense of the independent standing its supporters hoped to secure. Defiance would uphold the claim of a separate republic and rally those unwilling to accept British supervision. It would also worsen relations with the power best placed to decide whether the experiment is allowed to continue.
Seek an accommodation with the British authorities.
The raad must uphold its claim to independence.

The restored republic at Swellendam invokes the district revolt of 1795, when local grievances briefly broke the authority of the old colonial administration. Its new leaders now face a question that a remembered rebellion cannot answer: who is entitled to speak for the district today? An open assembly would give more of its inhabitants a hearing and help ease resentment against rule by a few established families. Those families argue that their experience and standing are precisely what keep the district together. This revival of republican government must choose whether its founding memory supports a broader public life or a return to familiar local patrons.
Open the assembly to a wider public.

A republican raad once again sits at Graaff-Reinet, claiming the legacy of the district's rebellion against colonial authority. The eastern frontier, however, cannot be governed through that memory alone. Farmers, traders and Xhosa communities bring conflicting claims to land, movement and security. A frontier commission could hear disputes and seek agreements before an isolated incident draws in the commandos. Expansionists consider such restraint a weakness, insisting that the restored government must defend its own settlers' claims first. The choice will help determine whether our neighbours see a possible negotiating partner or another administration preparing to advance the frontier.
Send a commission to negotiate the frontier disputes.
Put the settlers' frontier claims first.

The arrival of diamond prospectors has made Griqua authority more valuable and more vulnerable at the same time. Diggers and merchants want access to the fields, while outside governments examine every disputed boundary for an opportunity to intervene. Licences issued through the council would affirm that mineral wealth is subject to local government and provide a basis for collecting revenue. A long concession would bring money more quickly, but place much of the initiative in the hands of its holders. The council must decide whether the rush will strengthen its institutions or leave them dependent on an agreement negotiated under immediate financial pressure.
Make the prospectors answer to the council.
Sell a concession to secure immediate funds.

The migration east has brought the Griqua community to a new centre at Kokstad, but arrival is only the beginning of rebuilding. Families need shelter, dependable stores and routes linking their farms to the town. A functioning capital would give the administration a place to keep records and organise assistance after the demands of the journey. Others argue that herds and grazing must come first: a town cannot feed its inhabitants if the pastoral economy is neglected. With limited resources available, the council must decide whether to begin with public construction or leave households to establish themselves around their livestock.
Build the stores and services of our new capital.
Give priority to the herds and grazing economy.

A constitution promises orderly government, but people living far from the capital experience that promise through the district officials who hear their disputes. Questions of land, labour and debt may be decided by men closely connected to the families bringing the cases. Regular circuit courts would carry a more consistent authority into the countryside and offer a check on local influence. Judges, travel and records would all have to be paid for. The cheaper course is to trust the landdrosts already in place, accepting that the strength of a written rule may continue to depend on whose district applies it.
Carry the courts into every district.
Trust the existing landdrosts to administer justice.
The Rand and the rural treasury

The Rand has changed the scale of the republic's finances. Mining revenue offers possibilities that a treasury supported by scattered farms could scarcely consider, yet it has also sharpened disagreement about whom the state serves. Mine workers and rural households do not share equally in the new wealth, while public services struggle to keep pace with growth. Investing part of the receipts would help the government adapt to this new economy. Keeping a reserve would preserve financial room for future emergencies and reassure burghers suspicious of a larger state. The raad must decide how much of the mining boom should be turned into public capacity now.
Put part of the mining revenue into public works.
Build a reserve before expanding expenditure.

Petitions reaching the Natalia raad describe a country much larger than its circle of enfranchised burghers. African communities seek decisions about residence, grazing and land, often through intermediaries whose account may be the only one officials hear. Providing interpreters and a regular hearing would make those grievances harder to dismiss, while requiring the raad to acknowledge obligations beyond its own electorate. Restricting hearings to burghers would preserve the existing political order and cost less to administer. It would also leave much of the population without a recognised way to challenge the decisions that shape its daily life.
Hear the petitions with interpreters present.
Reserve the raad's hearings for the burghers.

The New Republic's officials are asked to issue land titles faster than they can establish the boundaries those titles describe. Settlers expect the promises that brought them here to be honoured, while neighbouring Zulu communities retain their own understanding of the same country. A survey before registration would slow the process and require public money, but might prevent incompatible claims from acquiring official seals. Accelerating the grants would satisfy impatient supporters of the republic. It would leave later officials to deal with disputes made harder by the government's own written commitments.
Survey the land before granting titles.
Issue the grants and settle boundaries later.

Winburg and Potchefstroom have joined their governments, but the Vaal still separates districts with their own leaders, accounts and expectations. A decision accepted by one raad may be regarded by the other as interference in local affairs. A stronger federal assembly could give these differences a common forum and make the union's authority more than the personal standing of its leading commandants. Concentrating power in the executive would promise quicker decisions, though at the cost of a narrower political voice. The united emigrant government must decide how it will command allegiance from districts accustomed to governing themselves.
Give the districts a stronger common assembly.
Strengthen the executive of the union.

At Philippolis, the council must weigh immediate financial pressure against the security of land used by the wider Griqua community. Settler demand has made leases attractive to individuals who need money, but overlapping promises can erode grazing arrangements on which many households depend. Defending communal agreements would require the administration to spend resources recording and upholding them. Accepting short leases would bring cash more quickly, while leaving the council to answer those who fear that temporary arrangements will become permanent losses. The decision concerns the basis of the community's livelihood as much as the balance of its treasury.
Accept leases to meet the immediate expense.

A trek moves only as fast as its weakest wagon. Broken axles, worn harness and exhausted oxen can hold a whole party beside a river crossing, while food must still be prepared and livestock watched. Much of that daily burden falls on women and family labour, far from a dependable workshop or market. Transport riders now propose shared repair stores and a reserve of equipment along the routes we use. The treasury would meet the initial expense, easing the cost of provisioning our commandos as well as civilian journeys. Others would leave every household to make its own arrangements: cheaper for the government today, but with little coordination when wagons and supplies are urgently needed.
Fund workshops and shared repair stores.
Each household must provision its own wagons.

Schooling in the farming districts often begins with a congregation, a borrowed room and a teacher supported by local households. That arrangement reaches some children well and leaves others far from any regular instruction. Public assistance could help sustain teachers and widen access beyond the families best able to pay. It would also draw the raad into questions about the curriculum and who is entitled to attend. Leaving education to the congregations would preserve familiar local control and demand less from the treasury. The choice is between extending public responsibility and relying on institutions whose strength varies greatly from district to district.
Help schools reach more of our children.
Leave education in the congregations' hands.

Transport riders have long carried the produce of inland farms to distant markets, following routes sustained by oxen, local knowledge and patience. As the railhead approaches, merchants anticipate cheaper deliveries, while riders fear losing the traffic that supports their teams and households. Cooperatives could help them organise feeder services and adapt their businesses to the railway instead of competing with it along the entire route. Such a transition would need public assistance. Leaving the adjustment to the market would spare that expense, but the gains from faster transport would come with disruption for those whose livelihoods were built around the wagon road.
Help the riders organise feeder cooperatives.
Let trade find its own arrangements.

The return of peace has not restored the livestock, equipment and savings lost by rural households. A farm may have an owner again and still lack the means to support a family. Requests for seed, tools and assistance reach an administration anxious to put its finances in order after years of disruption. A reconstruction programme would draw down scarce funds, but give struggling households a better chance of rebuilding their lives. Strict economy would protect the treasury and leave recovery to private resources. For families already burdened by debt, that distinction may determine whether returning home is a beginning or another disappointment.
Help households rebuild their farms and homes.
The treasury must recover before it can assist.

Afrikaans is increasingly present in print, classrooms and public debate, challenging the distance between the language many people speak and the language expected in official business. Recognition would bring government closer to those speakers, but the country contains communities using other languages as well. Funding translation alongside the change would help keep courts and schools accessible across that divide. A narrower programme would concentrate resources on standardising official usage and offer a clearer symbol of national identity. The raad must decide whether linguistic recognition will be accompanied by practical access for people outside its preferred language.
Recognise Afrikaans and retain translation services.
Make Afrikaans the common administrative standard.

The Cape constitutional settlement raises the relationship between property qualifications, political rights and racial exclusion. Extending practical access requires registration, courts and schooling.

Dutch rule at the Cape in this campaign is an alternate history. Restoring commercial ties with the Netherlands creates choices over language, local representation and the position of existing communities.

German expansion along the southwest African coast requires supplies and agreements over land. Treating local communities as parties to negotiation may restrain concession holders seeking sweeping rights.

Union joins administrations with different laws, languages and political traditions. The settlement also excludes much of the population from power. Public services can address some grievances, although they cannot by themselves resolve political exclusion.
Our republic is a dependent state. The local elective constitution remains in force, with a distinct dependency flag. Independence restores the ordinary republican government.
The end of our dependent status restores the sovereign republican flag and ordinary democratic government.
